name: Multi-Device Scheduling and Aperture-Sharing Benchmark
description: This paper presents two related benchmark studies of AI-enabled wireless power transfer (WPT) for FR3 (7–24 GHz) ultra-massive MIMO (UM-MIMO) 6G base stations. Study 1 benchmarks time-slotted WPT scheduling across multiple IoT devices, comparing naive, sustainability-aware, round-robin and proportional-fair policies with a learned time-to-depletion predictor. Across 80 randomized 15-device populations, naive battery-priority scheduling saved none of the 238 physically sustainable devices, sustainability awareness raised the save rate to 23.5%, and a proportional-fair policy weighted by harvesting surplus performed best (51.7%), ahead of the learned predictor (42.4%). Study 2 asks whether an array should share its aperture between communication and WPT by partitioning its elements (power-splitting) or by alternating between the two functions in time (time-switching) under time-varying battery and queue demand. Power-splitting yielded shorter communication queues at every tested distance, and at 5 m, adaptive power-splitting avoided battery depletion in all 40 trials, whereas fixed allocation depleted the battery in every trial; adaptivity provided no such benefit under time-switching. Together, the studies indicate that the aperture-sharing architecture sets the achievable ceiling and the scheduling policy determines how close a deployment comes to it, so the architecture decision should be made first.
